metadata.title: Southwest Florida Plant Guide
metadata.description: Comprehensive plant reference guide for Southwest Florida covering native, beneficial non-native, edible, and invasive plants across 15 categories.

plants.description: The single most ecologically important tree you can plant in SW Florida. Supports hundreds of caterpillar and moth species — critical food for nesting birds. Acorns feed squirrels, deer, turkeys, blue jays, and woodpeckers year-round. Massive spreading canopy provides prime nesting sites for eagles, owls, and songbirds. Long-lived, hurricane resistant, and deeply beautiful. Give it significant room — it spreads as wide as it is tall.
plants.growth_notes: Slow in first 1-2 years while establishing root system, then accelerates
plants.pruning_notes: Prune only dead or damaged wood. Never top a live oak — it permanently damages the tree and creates dangerous deadwood.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Once established, live oak is essentially indestructible in SW Florida. The challenge is patience — it takes years to establish.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Keystone species supporting hundreds of insect species, cavity nesters, acorn producers, and canopy habitat. Maximum ecological value.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect acorns when they fall naturally. Plant immediately — acorns lose viability quickly. Plant 1 inch deep in sandy soil.
plants.germination_notes: Plant fresh acorns immediately after collection — viability drops significantly after 2-4 weeks
plants.transplant_notes: Buy smallest available container size — live oaks transplant better when small. Stake for first year. Water deeply weekly for first full year regardless of rainfall.
do_not_plant_near: Structures, driveways, and utilities — spreading root system and canopy require significant space. Minimum 20 ft from any structure.
plants.looks_like_plants: Turkey oak (Quercus laevis), water oak (Quercus nigra)
plants.looks_like_notes: Other Florida oaks are similar but live oak is the only evergreen oak. The rounded lobed leaves and spreading horizontal canopy are distinctive.
plants.attracts_specific: Blue jay (primary acorn disperser), Red-headed woodpecker, Pileated woodpecker (cavity), Great horned owl (nesting), Eastern screech owl, Hundreds of Lepidoptera species as host plant

seasonal_care.january: No action needed. Brief leaf drop and replacement happens now.
seasonal_care.february: Light leaf drop continues — normal, not a disease. Do not rake aggressively.
seasonal_care.march: New leaf flush. Best time for any necessary structural pruning.
seasonal_care.april: Full canopy established. No action needed.
seasonal_care.may: Monitor for oak galls — unsightly but not harmful, no treatment needed.
seasonal_care.july: Monitor for any storm damage to branches.
seasonal_care.october: Peak acorn drop. Prime food source for wildlife.
seasonal_care.november: Acorn drop continues. Best planting month for new oaks.

common_problems.symptoms: Round or irregular growths on leaves or twigs — can look alarming
common_problems.solution: Caused by tiny wasps — completely harmless to the tree. No treatment needed or recommended. The galls are a food source for some wildlife.

common_problems.symptoms: Individual branches dying back suddenly, especially after storm damage
common_problems.solution: Remove dead branches promptly to prevent pest entry. Paint cut surfaces with wound dressing. If multiple branches affected, contact a certified arborist — may indicate bacterial infection.

common_problems.problem: Resurrection fern browning in dry weather
common_problems.symptoms: Fern on bark turns brown and appears dead
common_problems.solution: Not a problem — this is normal behavior for resurrection fern. It will return to vivid green within hours of rainfall.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. Buy the smallest container size available for best transplant success.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at most nurseries throughout Lee and Collier counties
plants.expert_tips: The most important thing to know about live oak is that the root system spreads 2-3x the canopy width underground. Plant it once, plant it right, and give it room. A live oak planted in the wrong spot is a problem that compounds for decades. When in doubt, plant it further from the house than you think you need to.
plants.fun_fact: A single mature live oak can support over 500 species of caterpillars and moths — more than almost any other tree in the Eastern United States. Those caterpillars are the primary food source for nesting songbirds.
plants.traditional_uses: Acorns were a staple food for the Calusa people of SW Florida. The dense hardwood was prized for shipbuilding — USS Constitution ('Old Ironsides') was built largely from live oak timber.
plants.conservation_notes: Live oak hammocks are a critically threatened habitat in SW Florida due to development. Each mature live oak supports a unique ecosystem. Lee and Collier counties protect mature specimens — check local ordinances before any work near a large live oak.

plants.description: Iconic tourist tree with striking peeling red-copper bark. One of SW Florida's fastest growing native trees and exceptionally hurricane resistant. Small fruits eaten by many birds. Extremely drought and salt tolerant. Great for quick canopy cover.

plants.description: Native pine critical to Florida's flatwood ecosystem. Seeds eaten by doves, quail, squirrels, and many songbirds. Host tree for numerous moth and butterfly larvae. Essential cavity nesting sites for woodpeckers, owls, and flying squirrels. Perfectly suited to Cape Coral's well-drained sandy substrate.

plants.description: Majestic native for wet areas, canal edges, and pond margins. Seeds eaten by wood ducks, sandhill cranes, and many birds. Important nesting habitat for ospreys, herons, and owls. Cypress knees create unique microhabitat. Stunning russet-orange fall color. Extremely long-lived.

plants.description: Native holly producing masses of bright red berries that cedar waxwings, robins, and mockingbirds devour in winter. Tolerates wet areas well. Can be grown as a large shrub or small tree. Female plants need a nearby male for berry production.
warnings: Berries are toxic to humans and pets — do not ingest.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth, faster in moist sites
plants.pruning_notes: Minimal pruning needed. Shape lightly in spring.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Tolerates wet areas, drought, and salt. Very adaptable.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, winter berry food source for birds, nesting habitat
plants.propagation_seed: Collect berries when ripe red. Clean pulp. Cold stratify 60-90 days before sowing.
plants.germination_method: Cold stratify then sow in moist mix
plants.germination_notes: Cold stratification greatly improves germination
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well from container. Tolerates wet planting sites. Plant male and female for berries.
plants.looks_like_notes: Dahoon holly identified by clusters of bright red berries, narrow lance-shaped leaves, and tolerance of wet sites. Inkberry (I. glabra) has black berries and is also native.
plants.attracts_specific: Cedar waxwing (primary winter berry consumer), American robin, Hermit thrush, Gray catbird

common_problems.symptoms: Flowers but no berry production
common_problems.solution: Dahoon holly is dioecious — separate male and female plants required. Ensure at least one male plant within 50 ft of female plants. Wind and bees transfer pollen.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries throughout SW Florida.
plants.expert_tips: Plant male and female together for berry production — this is the most commonly overlooked requirement. One male will pollinate several females within range.
plants.fun_fact: Cedar waxwings eat the berries so quickly that the display can last only days when a flock arrives. Plant multiple specimens to extend the food supply.
plants.traditional_uses: Berries used in folk medicine by various cultures for their emetic properties. Not recommended for consumption.
plants.conservation_notes: Dahoon holly is one of the most important winter food plants for migrating birds in SW Florida. Populations have declined with the loss of wetland habitats.

plants.description: One of the most bird-attractive fruiting trees in Florida. Rose-breasted grosbeaks, scarlet tanagers, catbirds, and dozens of other species flock to it during fruiting in spring. Berries also eaten by raccoons, opossums, and foxes. Edible for humans — sweet and abundant.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing fruit tree
plants.pruning_notes: Prune after fruiting season to control size. Annual pruning encourages new fruiting wood.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy in SW Florida. Tolerates range of conditions.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, major spring bird food source, mammals, dual food garden and wildlife value
plants.propagation_seed: Seeds germinate readily but fruiting quality variable. Buy named varieties for best fruit.
plants.propagation_cutting: Softwood cuttings in spring. Moderately difficult.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in well-drained mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates better than stored.
plants.transplant_notes: Container plants transplant well. Provide plenty of space — trees spread wide. Berry drop will stain pavement.
do_not_plant_near: Paved areas, driveways, light-colored surfaces — falling berries cause significant staining
plants.looks_like_notes: White mulberry was introduced and has naturalized in some areas. Red mulberry has slightly larger leaves with a rough upper surface. White mulberry leaves are smoother and glossier.
plants.attracts_specific: Rose-breasted grosbeak (major consumer), Scarlet tanager, Gray catbird, Northern mockingbird, American robin, Cedar waxwing, Raccoon, Opossum, Fox squirrel

common_problems.symptoms: Purple-red stains on surfaces below tree
common_problems.solution: Plant away from any paved areas or light-colored surfaces. The staining is difficult to remove. Plan placement carefully — the berries are a feature, not a bug.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Red mulberry is less commonly available than the non-native white mulberry — verify species.
plants.expert_tips: Red mulberry has one of the most concentrated wildlife feeding events of any SW Florida tree. When it fruits in spring, the sheer number and variety of bird species visiting can be extraordinary — it's worth planting in a visible spot from your home for the spring bird watching alone.
plants.fun_fact: Red mulberry is the host plant for the silkworm moth — though the commercial silk industry uses white mulberry. Red mulberry silk was used by some Native American peoples.
plants.traditional_uses: Berries eaten fresh and used for jams, jellies, pies, and wine by Native American peoples and European settlers. The wood was used for fence posts and furniture.
plants.conservation_notes: Red mulberry populations have declined in the Southeast due to displacement by the invasive white mulberry and hybridization between the two species. Planting true red mulberry supports the native species.

plants.description: Fast-growing native that works as a large shrub or small multi-trunk tree. Waxy gray berries are the primary winter food source for yellow-rumped warblers and many other migrating birds. Nitrogen-fixer that improves soil health. Highly salt tolerant and adaptable.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Native fruiting tree whose sweet fall fruits feed bluebirds, mockingbirds, warblers, raccoons, foxes, and deer. Edible for humans after fruits fully ripen — unripe fruits are very astringent. Host tree for luna moth and royal walnut moth caterpillars.
warnings: Unripe fruits are extremely astringent — wait until fully soft and ripe before eating.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Evergreen native with blue-gray berries eaten by many birds — cedar waxwings are literally named for this tree. Dense fragrant foliage provides year-round nesting cover. Very salt and drought tolerant. Often protected under county tree ordinances.
warnings: Often protected by county ordinances — check local regulations before removing mature specimens.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: One of the most wildlife-productive trees in Florida — fruit eaten by 28+ bird species. Supports enormous insect diversity. Begins life as an epiphyte before becoming a freestanding tree. Protected tree in many FL counties.
warnings: Roots are very aggressive near hardscape and foundations. Plant well away from structures. Protected tree in many counties — check before removing.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Classic coastal native highly tolerant of salt, wind, and drought. A keystone of SW Florida's coastal hammock habitat. Can be maintained as a clipped formal hedge or allowed to grow into an attractive multi-trunk tree.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate to fast growth. Very adaptable.
plants.pruning_notes: Excellent hedge plant. Can be sheared to any size or allowed to grow naturally. Very tolerant of hard pruning.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the most adaptable and tough native plants for SW Florida coastal conditions.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, coastal habitat keystone, caterpillar host, bird seeds and nesting, hurricane tough
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seed heads when brown. Sow in sandy well-drained mix.
plants.germination_notes: Good germination rate in well-drained conditions.
plants.transplant_notes: Extremely easy to transplant. Very forgiving. Tolerates salt spray, wind, poor soil, and drought from day one.
plants.looks_like_notes: The spongy button-like seed heads in clusters are distinctive. The small dark leathery leaves and tolerance of coastal conditions make it recognizable.
plants.attracts_specific: Mangrove cuckoo (nesting), White-crowned pigeon (seeds), Migratory warblers (insects in canopy)

common_problems.problem: Chlorosis in non-coastal high pH soils
common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing leaves despite good water
common_problems.solution: Buttonwood actually prefers alkaline coastal conditions. Chlorosis rare in its preferred coastal habitat. If occurring, verify drainage is adequate.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida native nurseries and coastal landscaping specialists.
plants.expert_tips: Buttonwood is one of very few native plants that bridges upland and mangrove zones. It can be planted right at the edge of mangrove habitat where almost nothing else will grow, and it establishes a transition zone that supports both upland and wetland wildlife.
plants.fun_fact: Buttonwood is considered the landward edge of the mangrove zone — it bridges the gap between terrestrial and marine ecosystems, one of the most biologically productive transition zones on earth.
plants.traditional_uses: The dense hard wood was used for charcoal production and fuel wood historically. The charcoal was considered exceptionally high quality.
plants.conservation_notes: Buttonwood is a key component of SW Florida's coastal hammock habitat, one of the most threatened ecosystems in the region due to sea level rise and development.

plants.description: Iconic coastal native with huge round leathery leaves and grape-like fruit clusters. Fruits are edible for humans — used in jams and jellies — and eaten by many birds and mammals. Extremely salt and drought tolerant.
warnings: Protected by Florida statute near coastlines — trimming may require permits. Check local regulations before pruning.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth. Faster in full sun.
plants.pruning_notes: Can be maintained as a hedge or small tree. Hard prune tolerant.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy in coastal SW Florida. Extremely salt and drought tolerant.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, edible fruit for humans and wildlife, coastal habitat value, large ornamental leaves
plants.propagation_seed: Plant fresh berries directly in sandy soil. Remove pulp first.
plants.propagation_cutting: Semi-hardwood cuttings root in warm conditions.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates much better than dried.
plants.transplant_notes: Very easy to transplant. Tolerates full coastal exposure immediately after planting. Salt spray does not harm it.
plants.looks_like_notes: Sea grape has the largest and most distinctive leaves of any common coastal tree — huge round leathery leaves with red veins. Pigeon plum has smaller narrower leaves. Sea grape is unmistakable.
plants.attracts_specific: White-crowned pigeon (primary fruit consumer — this pigeon depends heavily on sea grape), Northern mockingbird, Raccoon, White-tailed deer

seasonal_care.april: Flowering — small fragrant white flowers on long racemes

common_problems.symptoms: N/A — regulatory issue not a plant problem
common_problems.solution: Sea grape is protected by Florida statute in coastal areas. Trimming seagrape seaward of the coastal construction control line requires a permit from the Florida DEP. Always check permit requirements before any pruning near the coast.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries. One of the most popular native coastal plants.
plants.expert_tips: Sea grape jelly is a genuine SW Florida culinary tradition. The grapes are small with large seeds but the jelly has a unique mild fruity flavor worth making. Harvest when the clusters turn deep purple-black — taste one first to check ripeness.
plants.fun_fact: Sea grape leaves have been used as natural plates and writing surfaces — the large leathery leaves can be written on with a stick or nail, earning the plant its folk name 'sea grape paper.'
plants.traditional_uses: Fruit eaten fresh and made into jelly and wine throughout the Caribbean. Bark and leaves used medicinally in traditional Caribbean medicine.
plants.conservation_notes: Sea grape is one of the defining plants of SW Florida's coastal landscape. Its populations are declining due to coastal development and sea level rise, making each cultivated specimen an act of conservation.
plants.hoa_notes: Protected by Florida statute near coastlines — HOAs cannot require removal in protected zones.

plants.description: One of SW Florida's most spectacular small native trees. Clusters of vivid orange trumpet flowers bloom nearly year-round and are a magnet for hummingbirds and bees. Very salt and drought tolerant. Stays relatively small at 15-25 ft — perfect for smaller yards.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth. Flowers continuously once established.
plants.pruning_notes: Prune lightly after heavy bloom cycles to maintain size.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the most rewarding small native trees for SW Florida. Drought and salt tolerant.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, year-round hummingbird magnet, bee forage, bird food, small size ideal for residential
plants.propagation_seed: Collect white drupes when soft and ripe. Clean and sow fresh.
plants.propagation_cutting: Semi-hardwood cuttings root in warm conditions.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed performs much better than dried.
plants.transplant_notes: Excellent transplant tolerance. Plant in fall for best establishment. Does not need irrigation after first few months.
plants.looks_like_notes: The native Geiger tree has distinctive rough-textured dark green leaves and brilliant orange flowers. Unmistakable when in bloom.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (primary pollinator), Broad-tailed hummingbird (winter visitor), Honeybees, White-crowned pigeon (fruit)

common_problems.problem: Leaf scorch in full coastal exposure
common_problems.symptoms: Brown leaf edges in salt spray areas
common_problems.solution: Geiger tree is among the most salt tolerant natives but extreme direct spray can cause temporary leaf scorch. Recovery is rapid. No treatment needed.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries throughout SW Florida. Worth seeking out — not always at big box stores.
plants.expert_tips: The Geiger tree is named for John Geiger, a 19th-century Key West pilot and wrecker who had a large specimen growing at his home. It remains an iconic plant of Florida's coastal communities. Plant one near a window where you can see hummingbirds.
plants.fun_fact: The Geiger tree is the unofficial symbol of Key West and appears in John James Audubon's famous painting of the white-crowned pigeon feeding on its fruit during his 1832 visit to Florida.
plants.traditional_uses: The bark has been used medicinally in Caribbean folk medicine for chest complaints and coughs.
plants.conservation_notes: The native Geiger tree is increasingly rare in SW Florida's natural coastal hammocks due to development. Each cultivated specimen preserves the species in the landscape.

plants.description: Florida's native mahogany — a beautiful broad canopy tree of South Florida's tropical hardwood hammocks. Seeds in large woody pods eaten by parrots and other birds. Host plant for several moth species. Semi-deciduous in late winter.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth. Long-lived and increasingly beautiful with age.
plants.pruning_notes: Remove dead wood only. Do not top. Shape lightly if needed.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Requires good drainage and full sun. More specific needs than some natives.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, seed food for parrots and birds, host plant, semi-deciduous spectacle
plants.propagation_seed: Collect winged seeds from pods before pods open fully. Sow fresh in sandy mix.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh winged seeds in well-drained sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Germination typically good when fresh. Seeds lose viability quickly.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants reasonably well when young. Very difficult as a large specimen. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage.
do_not_plant_near: Low wet areas — does not tolerate waterlogged conditions
plants.looks_like_notes: Florida native mahogany is distinguished by its smaller leaves and seed pods compared to the Central American species. The peeling gray bark and semi-deciduous habit in late winter are identifying features.
plants.attracts_specific: Cuban amazon parrot (seeds — historically), Red-bellied woodpecker (insects in bark), Various moth species (host plant)

common_problems.problem: Poor growth in wet or alkaline soils
common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing, poor growth, dieback
common_problems.solution: Florida mahogany requires excellent drainage and performs best in slightly acidic sandy soil. Alkaline muck or clay soils significantly reduce performance. Plant in native sandy substrate.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Less commonly available than many other natives.
plants.expert_tips: Florida mahogany is essentially the only native tree in North America producing the famous fine-grained furniture wood. Old-growth specimens were logged to near extinction — planting one is a genuine conservation act and a multi-generational gift.
plants.fun_fact: USS Constitution, the world's oldest commissioned naval vessel still afloat, was built largely from live oak and Florida mahogany. The wood's strength and beauty made it the most valuable timber in the New World.
plants.traditional_uses: The wood has been one of the most prized furniture woods in the world for centuries. Seminole people used the wood for tools and implements.
plants.conservation_notes: Florida native mahogany is listed as endangered in the wild in South Florida due to historical logging and current development. The Big Cypress and Everglades areas hold the remaining natural populations.

plants.description: Small native tree with intensely fragrant golden-yellow puffball flowers in late winter and spring when little else is blooming — a critical early nectar source for bees and butterflies. Very drought tolerant. Thorny habit provides excellent protected nesting cover.
warnings: Has sharp thorns — plant away from high foot traffic areas.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing small tree
plants.pruning_notes: Remove dead wood. Light shaping acceptable. Avoid pruning when bees actively foraging on flowers.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy and drought tolerant. The thorns require thoughtful siting.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, critical early spring bee food, butterfly forage, protective nesting cover from thorns
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seed pods when dry. Scarify seeds or soak in hot water 24hr before sowing.
plants.propagation_cutting: Not commonly done. Seed is easier.
plants.germination_method: Sow scarified seed in sandy well-drained mix
plants.germination_notes: Hard seed coat requires scarification for reliable germination.
plants.transplant_notes: Easy to transplant when young. Site away from foot traffic areas due to thorns. Excellent for property boundaries.
do_not_plant_near: Walkways, play areas, pet areas — the thorns are very sharp
plants.looks_like_notes: Sweet acacia identified by its small bipinnate leaves, intensely fragrant golden pompom flowers in late winter, and sharp thorns. The fragrance in late winter is remarkable — one of the most perfumed native plants in SW Florida.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybees (critical early spring nectar source), Native bees, Gulf fritillary butterfly, Cloudless sulphur butterfly, Nesting birds (protected by thorns)

seasonal_care.march: Flowering — peak fragrance. Peak bee activity. Do not prune.

common_problems.symptoms: Puncture wounds from thorns
common_problems.solution: Prevention through siting. Plant at least 6 ft from walkways and pet areas. Wear heavy gloves during any pruning.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Less common at big box stores.
plants.expert_tips: Sweet acacia blooms in late winter when virtually nothing else is flowering in SW Florida — it is a critical early-season food source for bees emerging from slower winter months. The fragrance is used in real perfumery — the species is one of the sources of cassie absolute, a traditional perfume ingredient.
plants.fun_fact: Sweet acacia (Vachellia farnesiana) is named for Cardinal Odoardo Farnese, who grew one in his Roman garden in the early 1600s. The fragrance is used in high-end perfumery and has been for centuries.
plants.traditional_uses: Used throughout history as a source of perfume (cassie absolute) and gum arabic. Pods and seeds eaten by indigenous peoples. Bark used medicinally.
plants.conservation_notes: A native of SW Florida's pine flatwood and scrub edges, sweet acacia populations have declined with habitat loss. Its thorns make it excellent wildlife habitat — small birds nest in the protected branches away from predators.

plants.description: One of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world — explosively covered in brilliant orange-red blooms in early summer. A defining tree of SW Florida's landscape. Fast-growing with a broad flat canopy providing excellent shade. Non-native but low ecological risk.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets if large quantities of seeds are ingested — monitor pets around fallen seed pods.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Iconic tropical tree with intensely fragrant flowers in white, pink, yellow, red, and multicolor. One of the most planted ornamentals in SW Florida. Very drought tolerant. Goes briefly deciduous in winter.
warnings: Toxic to pets — milky sap causes vomiting, diarrhea, and skin irritation in dogs and cats. Keep pets away from fallen flowers and branches.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Spectacular flowering trees that put on a jaw-dropping show of pink, yellow, or white trumpet blooms in spring — often before the leaves emerge. Bees and hummingbirds visit the flowers. Drought tolerant once established.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Very popular non-native with distinctive bright red brush-like flower spikes. Hummingbirds and bees adore the flowers. Drought and salt tolerant. Can be grown as a large shrub or trained into a multi-trunk tree up to 25 ft.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Extremely popular ornamental tree with showy summer blooms in pink, red, white, and purple. Bees visit the flowers actively. Attractive peeling bark and fall color. Very drought tolerant. One of the most commonly planted trees in SW Florida.
warnings: Avoid heavy topping — it destroys the natural form and weakens the tree. Prune lightly or not at all.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Florida's state tree and a true ecological keystone. Berries are a critical food source for robins, cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, raccoons, and many other species. Old frond boots provide essential nesting habitat for owls, bats, and cavity-nesting birds. Highly fragrant flowers attract bees. Extremely hurricane and salt tolerant.
warnings: Edible heart-of-palm — but harvesting kills the tree. Never harvest from wild or landscape specimens.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Arguably the most ecologically important shrub-palm in SW Florida. Berries are a critical food source for black bears, deer, raccoons, gopher tortoises, and dozens of bird species. Flowers are among Florida's most important bee plants. Dense colonies provide irreplaceable wildlife cover.
warnings: Serrated leaf stems cause cuts — handle with heavy gloves.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: Generally acceptable in naturalistic settings. May conflict with HOAs requiring manicured appearance.

plants.description: Florida's most spectacular native palm — tall, straight, and regal with a smooth cement-gray trunk and a vivid green crownshaft. Small dark fruits eaten by many birds including parrots and pigeons. Fast growing for a palm. Surprisingly hurricane resistant.
warnings: Endangered in the wild — buy only nursery-grown specimens.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: The ultimate tropical icon. Coconuts are edible for humans and the fruits, flowers, and fronds all support wildlife. Very salt tolerant. Fast growing and striking. Available in Malayan dwarf varieties that stay lower and produce earlier.
warnings: Falling coconuts are a genuine hazard — plant away from seating areas, walkways, and parked cars. Remove nuts regularly in high-traffic areas.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: Some HOAs restrict coconut palms near property lines due to falling coconut hazard.

plants.description: Not actually a palm at all — a cycad. Extremely popular in SW Florida landscapes for its neat symmetrical form. However it is one of the most dangerously toxic plants to dogs and cats in existence. Virtually no wildlife value.
warnings: HIGHLY TOXIC — one of the most poisonous plants to pets in Florida. All parts are toxic; seeds are extremely dangerous and can cause liver failure and death in dogs and cats. Avoid entirely if pets have yard access.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: The king of SW Florida fruit trees. Thrives in Cape Coral's heat and humidity. Grafted trees fruit in 2-3 years. Prune annually after harvest to control size and promote production. Watch for anthracnose fungal disease during wet season.
warnings: Mango sap and skin can cause skin irritation in sensitive people. Mango pit and skin can cause digestive issues in pets — keep pits away from dogs.

varieties.name: Carrie
varieties.notes: One of the best backyard varieties — compact tree, incredibly rich flavor, no fiber. Self-pollinating. Early harvest May-June.

varieties.name: Cogshall
varieties.notes: Top condo mango — slow growing, very easy to control size. Perfect for small yards or containers. Fiberless, excellent flavor.

varieties.name: Nam Doc Mai
varieties.notes: Thai variety with sweet fragrant fiber-free fruit. Semi-dwarf, manageable size. July-August harvest.

varieties.name: Kent
varieties.notes: Considered one of the sweetest Florida mangoes. Large tree but excellent production. Late season harvest July-August.

varieties.name: Keitt
varieties.notes: Best late season variety — stays green when ripe. Large fruit, heat tolerant, excellent disease resistance. Harvest August-September.

plants.description: Excellent fruit tree for SW Florida in well-drained spots. West Indian varieties are best suited to Cape Coral's heat. Needs good drainage. Plant Type A and Type B varieties together for best pollination. Watch for laurel wilt disease.
warnings: Toxic to pets — the leaves, bark, skin, and pit contain persin which causes vomiting and diarrhea in dogs and cats. Keep fallen fruit picked up.

varieties.name: Choquette
varieties.notes: One of the most popular Florida backyard varieties. Large fruit up to 3 lbs, good flavor. Harvest November-January.

varieties.name: Monroe
varieties.notes: Large high-quality fruit with excellent flavor. Good disease resistance. Pairs well with Choquette for cross-pollination.

varieties.name: Brogdon
varieties.notes: Most cold-tolerant Florida variety. Medium fruit, good flavor. Harvest August-October.

varieties.name: Hall
varieties.notes: Excellent disease resistance — recommended by UF/IFAS. Good flavor, medium-large fruit. Harvest October-November.

varieties.name: Lula
varieties.notes: Classic Florida variety, cold tolerant, good production. Medium fruit with rich flavor. Harvest October-December.

plants.description: One of the best all-around wildlife shrubs for Southwest Florida. Tubular red-orange flowers bloom nearly year-round attracting hummingbirds and butterflies constantly. Dark berries eaten by many bird species. Host plant for the pluto sphinx moth. Important: only plant the true native Hamelia patens var. patens — not dwarf, African, or compacta varieties.
warnings: Do NOT buy dwarf, African, or compacta varieties — they are not native and have significantly less wildlife value.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: None — SW Florida rainfall sufficient once established

plants.growth_notes: Can reach 6 ft in first season under ideal conditions
plants.pruning_notes: Hard prune in spring to maintain size and encourage dense bushy growth
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the most forgiving native shrubs in SW Florida. Tolerates poor soil, drought, and neglect.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, supports 5+ wildlife categories, year-round host and nectar source
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe berries, clean pulp, sow fresh. Germination in 14-21 days.
plants.propagation_cutting: Softwood cuttings in spring-summer. Root in moist mix, 3-4 weeks.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates best — viability drops quickly
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants easily from container. Water well for first 2-3 weeks. Avoid transplanting in peak summer heat — fall is ideal in SW Florida.
plants.looks_like_plants: African firebush (Hamelia patens var. glabra), dwarf firebush, compacta firebush
plants.looks_like_notes: Dwarf, African, and compacta varieties look similar but are not native and have significantly less wildlife value. Always verify you are buying Hamelia patens var. patens.
plants.attracts_specific: Pluto sphinx moth (Xylophanes pluto) — host plant; Ruby-throated hummingbird; Gulf fritillary butterfly; Zebra longwing butterfly

seasonal_care.january: No action needed. Enjoy winter blooms.
seasonal_care.february: Good time to prune if size control needed before spring flush.
seasonal_care.march: Apply slow-release fertilizer if desired. New growth begins.
seasonal_care.april: Monitor for whitefly — treat with neem oil if needed.
seasonal_care.may: Peak growing season begins. Water weekly if no rain for 2+ weeks.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season begins — typically no irrigation needed.
seasonal_care.july: Monitor for fungal issues in humid conditions. Remove dead wood.
seasonal_care.august: Continue monitoring. Peak wildlife activity on berries and flowers.
seasonal_care.september: Berries abundant — peak bird attraction. Excellent planting month.
seasonal_care.october: Best time to plant new specimens. Fall planting season begins.
seasonal_care.november: Continue fall planting. Prune lightly if needed.
seasonal_care.december: No action needed. Hardy through SW Florida winters.

common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing leaves, sticky residue, white insects under leaves
common_problems.solution: Spray with neem oil solution weekly for 3 weeks. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill beneficial insects visiting the flowers.

common_problems.symptoms: Long bare stems with foliage only at tips, reduced flowering
common_problems.solution: Hard prune to 12-18 inches in late winter or early spring. Will rebound vigorously with dense bushy growth within 6-8 weeks.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida native plant nurseries. Ensure you buy Hamelia patens var. patens — not dwarf or African variety.
plants.where_to_buy_local: FNPS plant sales, native plant nurseries throughout Lee and Collier counties
plants.expert_tips: The single most common mistake with firebush is buying the wrong variety — African and dwarf forms are widely sold but have a fraction of the wildlife value. The true native grows large — plan for 6-8 ft and prune hard once a year rather than clipping constantly. Hummingbirds will find it within days of planting if they are in the area.
plants.fun_fact: Firebush berries contain compounds studied for antimicrobial and antioxidant properties. The Seminole people used the plant medicinally.
plants.traditional_uses: Used medicinally by indigenous peoples of Central and South America. Berries used in traditional beverages in some cultures.
plants.conservation_notes: Populations of the true native firebush are declining in the landscape trade as non-native varieties dominate nursery stock. Buying and planting the true native variety actively supports genetic conservation of the species in SW Florida.
plants.hoa_notes: Many SW Florida HOAs now accept native plants. Lee and Collier County have native plant provisions.

plants.description: Famous for its extraordinary clusters of metallic purple berries eaten by over 40 bird species and deer. Host plant for spring azure butterfly. Low maintenance — dies back and rebounds vigorously each season. Adaptable to sun through shade.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Widely planted for extraordinary drought and salt tolerance, fast growth, and showy flowers in pink, white, red, and yellow. However the toxicity is severe and demands serious thought before planting in home landscapes with children or pets.
warnings: HIGHLY TOXIC — all parts including sap, flowers, leaves, stems, and water in a vase containing oleander are extremely toxic to humans, pets, horses, and livestock. Smoke from burning branches is toxic. One of the most dangerous common landscape plants.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: Many HOAs restrict or ban oleander due to toxicity concerns near children.

plants.description: One of the most essential hummingbird and butterfly plants for Southwest Florida. Brilliant red spikes bloom nearly year-round. Self-seeds prolifically so you will always have more. Very drought tolerant and easy. Excellent companion to firebush and blue porterweed.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Florida's single best lawn-substitute groundcover. Host plant for common buckeye, phaon crescent, and white peacock butterflies. Tiny white-purple flowers attract native bees constantly. Seeds eaten by birds. Can be mowed. Handles light foot traffic. One of the most ecologically valuable plants per square foot in all of Southwest Florida.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: One of the absolute best native vines for Southwest Florida. Tubular red and orange flowers bloom nearly year-round and hummingbirds are completely unable to resist them. Red berries eaten by birds. Well-behaved unlike invasive Japanese honeysuckle. A must-have for any hummingbird garden.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: One of the most beloved native grasses in Florida. In fall the clouds of airy pink-purple flower plumes are absolutely stunning — glowing in late afternoon light. Seeds eaten by birds. Dense clumps provide cover for ground birds and lizards. Plant in drifts for maximum impact.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: The single most recommended native aquatic plant for Southwest Florida's canals, ponds, and wet areas. Vivid violet-blue flower spikes bloom nearly year-round. Bees and butterflies visit constantly. Seeds eaten by ducks and water birds. Dense colonies provide critical fish habitat. Edible — seeds eaten like buckwheat, young leaves cooked like spinach.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: Permanent water or saturated soil required

plants.growth_notes: Spreads readily by rhizomes to form dense beneficial colonies
plants.pruning_notes: Cut back to water level in late winter if needed to control spread. Division is easy and creates new plants.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the most reliable and easy aquatic natives for SW Florida. Plant it in shallow water or saturated soil and it does the rest.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, year-round bloomer, supports bees, butterflies, birds, fish habitat, edible, and canal-bank stabilizer
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seed heads when brown. Direct sow in wet soil or shallow water.
plants.propagation_cutting: Division of rhizomes in spring or fall. Each division with roots will establish quickly.
plants.propagation_division: Easy — divide clumps in spring. Most practical propagation method.
plants.germination_notes: Seeds need consistently wet conditions to germinate. Division is easier and faster.
plants.transplant_notes: Plant rhizomes or divisions directly into wet soil or shallow water up to 12 inches deep. No special care needed — simply keep roots wet.
plants.looks_like_notes: Water hyacinth is invasive and looks superficially similar when not in bloom. Pickerelweed has a lance-shaped leaf with a heart-shaped base; water hyacinth has rounded inflated leaf stalks. Never plant water hyacinth.
plants.attracts_specific: Wood duck (seeds), Anhinga (nesting cover), Purple gallinule (nesting and foraging), Native bees including bumble bees, Long-tailed skipper butterfly

seasonal_care.january: No action needed. May die back slightly in coolest weather — will rebound.
seasonal_care.february: Division and replanting can be done now if needed.
seasonal_care.march: Growth resumes strongly. Good time to divide and spread.
seasonal_care.september: Seed heads forming — important bird food source.
seasonal_care.november: Good time to divide and replant.
seasonal_care.december: May slow slightly but typically evergreen in SW Florida.

common_problems.symptoms: Distorted new growth, sticky residue, clusters of small insects on stems
common_problems.solution: Strong spray of water knocks them off. Natural predators like lady beetles usually control them without intervention. Neem oil if persistent.

common_problems.symptoms: Expanding beyond intended planting area
common_problems.solution: Division and removal of outer rhizomes in spring or fall. Rhizomes are easy to pull. Regular division also creates plants to share or expand elsewhere.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries and aquatic plant specialists throughout SW Florida. Occasionally at big box garden centers.
plants.where_to_buy_local: FNPS plant sales, aquatic nurseries in Lee and Collier counties
plants.expert_tips: Plant pickerelweed in masses rather than as individual specimens — a dense colony of 10-20 plants along a canal bank does far more ecological work than a single specimen. The combination of pickerelweed, duck potato, and alligator flag creates a complete native aquatic edge that stabilizes the bank, filters runoff, and supports a full range of wildlife.
plants.fun_fact: Pickerelweed flowers are trimorphic — the species produces three different flower forms with different arrangements of stamens and pistils to encourage cross-pollination between plants. This is rare in the plant world.
plants.traditional_uses: Young leaf stalks and seeds were eaten by Native Americans. Seeds can be eaten raw or roasted and ground into flour. Young leaves are edible cooked like spinach.
plants.conservation_notes: Pickerelweed colonies along SW Florida's canals provide critical water filtration, removing excess nutrients from runoff before they enter larger water bodies. Replacing invasive aquatic plants with pickerelweed actively improves water quality throughout the canal system.

plants.description: The most iconic epiphyte of the American South. Not a moss, not a parasite — a true flowering bromeliad. Critical nesting material for northern parulas, Baltimore orioles, and other birds. Indicator of clean air quality. Harmless to healthy trees. A living symbol of authentic Florida.
warnings: Spanish moss often harbors chiggers and redbugs — wear long sleeves and gloves when handling fresh fallen clumps.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Florida's most common native cactus and an ecological powerhouse. Large showy yellow flowers with red centers attract bees and butterflies. Red-purple fruits eaten by gopher tortoises, birds, deer, and small mammals. Entire plant is edible — pads, fruits, and flowers all used in cooking. Very drought and salt tolerant.
warnings: Glochids — tiny barbed bristles on pads and fruits — cause intense skin irritation and are nearly invisible. Always wear thick gloves when handling.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Florida's largest native terrestrial fern — bold arching fronds can reach 6-8 ft creating a dramatic tropical statement. Excellent groundcover under trees and in shaded areas. Provides dense wildlife cover for frogs, lizards, and ground birds. Very fast growing once established. Pet safe.
warnings: Do NOT confuse with invasive tuberous sword fern (N. cordifolia) or Asian sword fern (N. brownii). Native giant sword fern has double-toothed pinnae margins and no tubers on runners. Always verify scientific name at purchase.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: One of Southwest Florida's most magical native plants — white to pink lily flowers appear seemingly overnight after summer rains. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit the flowers. Naturalizes beautifully in lawns and garden beds spreading over time. A classic Florida native experience.
warnings: All parts toxic to humans and pets — bulbs especially dangerous containing lycorine alkaloids. Do not ingest.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Arguably the single most ecologically important weed in Florida. Butterflies and native bees swarm it constantly all year long — documented as one of the top three most important honeybee plants in the Southeast. Seeds eaten by birds. Edible leaves and flowers used as salad garnish. Let it grow wherever you can.
plants.management: Let grow freely or manage after blooming to limit spread. Worth keeping in every yard.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: The single most destructive invasive plant in Southwest Florida. Forms impenetrable dense thickets that completely displace native vegetation. Red berries look attractive but are mildly toxic and the tree provides almost no native wildlife value compared to the habitat it destroys. Now covers over 700,000 acres in South Florida. Remove immediately whenever found.
warnings: Sap causes severe skin and eye irritation — related to poison ivy. Wear gloves, eye protection, and long sleeves when handling. Berries toxic to pets. Smoke from burning is toxic.
plants.removal_method: Cut stems at ground level and immediately apply concentrated herbicide (triclopyr or glyphosate) to cut surface. DO NOT burn — smoke is toxic. Repeat treatments needed. Root system must be killed or it resprouts. Contact Lee or Collier County Extension for assistance.
plants.growth_notes: Extremely fast growing — can form dense thickets within 2-3 years if not immediately controlled
plants.pruning_notes: DO NOT PRUNE — cutting without immediately treating cut surface with herbicide causes vigorous resprouting
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Grows easily in any condition — this is part of why it is so destructive as an invasive.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Category 1 invasive. No native wildlife value. Actively destroys native habitat.
plants.germination_notes: Self-seeds prolifically — birds spread seeds throughout natural areas
plants.transplant_notes: DO NOT TRANSPLANT — invasive species. Remove and destroy all plants.
do_not_plant_near: This IS the plant to avoid — remove from property immediately
plants.looks_like_plants: Florida holly (common name used for this plant), Christmas berry
plants.looks_like_notes: Often sold under misleading common names like 'Florida holly.' The compound leaves with a distinctive turpentine smell when crushed, red berries in dense clusters, and rough gray bark are identifying features. If you smell turpentine when you crush a leaf — it is Brazilian pepper. Remove it.
plants.attracts_specific: Birds eat the berries and spread seeds into natural areas — this is how it spreads so effectively. The wildlife value does not offset the ecological damage.

seasonal_care.january: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.february: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.march: Remove any plants found on property. Spring flush makes new seedlings visible.
seasonal_care.april: Check for new seedlings from winter berry drop.
seasonal_care.may: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.june: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.july: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.august: Berries forming — remove before they ripen to prevent bird spread.
seasonal_care.september: Berries ripening — highest spread risk. Remove urgently.
seasonal_care.october: Peak berry production — urgent removal priority.
seasonal_care.november: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.december: Berries being consumed and spread by birds — check property for seedlings.

common_problems.symptoms: Vigorous new growth from cut stumps and roots within weeks of removal
common_problems.solution: Cut must be immediately treated with concentrated triclopyr or glyphosate applied directly to the cut surface within 60 seconds of cutting. Untreated cuts resprout more vigorously than before.

common_problems.problem: Skin and eye irritation during removal
common_problems.symptoms: Redness, burning, swelling from contact with sap
common_problems.solution: Wear gloves, long sleeves, eye protection, and closed shoes during all removal work. Wash exposed skin immediately with soap and water. Related to poison ivy — some people have severe reactions.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: DO NOT PURCHASE. Illegal to plant in Florida. If seen for sale, report to Florida Department of Agriculture.
plants.expert_tips: The most important thing to know: never cut Brazilian pepper without immediately treating the stump. A cut stump without herbicide will resprout 3-5 new stems for every one you cut — making the problem worse. Always have your herbicide ready before you make the first cut. Small seedlings under 12 inches can be pulled by hand — the root system is shallow when young.
plants.fun_fact: Brazilian pepper is related to cashew, mango, and poison ivy — all members of the Anacardiaceae family. This is why the sap causes skin irritation similar to poison ivy in sensitive individuals.
plants.traditional_uses: Used as a folk remedy in South America for various ailments — however the allergenic properties make self-treatment dangerous. Not recommended under any circumstances.
plants.conservation_notes: Brazilian pepper now covers over 700,000 acres of South Florida — more than any other invasive plant in the state. It costs Florida millions of dollars per year to control. Every plant removed from a private property directly contributes to protecting what remains of SW Florida's native ecosystems.

plants.description: Australian tree that has invaded over 500,000 acres of South Florida's wetlands. Drains wetlands by transpiring enormous amounts of water, converting sawgrass marshes and cypress swamps into melaleuca monocultures. Federally listed noxious weed. Remove immediately.
warnings: Do not burn standing melaleuca — heat triggers seed release from the canopy. One tree can release millions of seeds when burned.
plants.removal_method: Cut and immediately treat stump with concentrated herbicide. Hack and squirt method effective on larger trees. Biological control (Melaleuca snout beetle) available — contact SFWMD for current programs.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Free-floating plant from South America that can double its population in two weeks, completely choking canals, ponds, and waterways. Reduces oxygen in water killing fish. Blocks boat traffic. Has infested Florida waterways since the 1880s and costs the state millions annually to control. Never introduce to water features.
warnings: Removal requires permits for aquatic herbicide use in Florida waterways. Contact SFWMD before applying any chemical treatment to canals.
plants.removal_method: Physical removal by hand or equipment for small infestations. Aquatic herbicides (2,4-D, glyphosate labeled for aquatic use) for larger infestations — requires permits. Contact SFWMD for assistance with canal infestations.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Underused native understory tree related to blueberry. Delicate bell-shaped white spring flowers feed bees. Shiny blue-black fall berries attract birds. Bark flakes to reveal attractive reddish layers. Well adapted to Florida's sandy soils.
plants.growth_notes: Slow growing understory tree
plants.pruning_notes: Light shaping only. Does not require regular pruning.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Requires acidic sandy soil — fails in alkaline conditions common in SW Florida. Test soil before planting.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, bee forage, bird berries, attractive bark
plants.propagation_seed: Collect berries when ripe. Clean and sow in acidic sandy mix.
plants.germination_method: Sow in acidic sandy mix — pH critical
plants.germination_notes: Needs acidic conditions for germination. Alkaline water inhibits germination.
plants.transplant_notes: Requires acidic well-drained sandy soil. Amend planting hole with sulfur and peat to lower pH. Test soil pH before planting. Mulch with pine bark.
do_not_plant_near: Alkaline soil areas without pH amendment
plants.looks_like_notes: Sparkleberry has smaller leaves and more tree-like growth habit than blueberry. The distinctive flaking reddish bark on older specimens is identifying. Berries are smaller and less flavorful than cultivated blueberry.
plants.attracts_specific: Various thrushes (berries), Eastern bluebird (berries), Native bees (spring flowers)

seasonal_care.february: Flowering begins — small white bell-shaped flowers

common_problems.symptoms: Yellow leaves, stunted growth
common_problems.solution: Almost always caused by soil pH too high. Sparkleberry requires acidic soil (4.5-6.5). Apply sulfur to lower pH and use acidifying fertilizer. This is the most common reason sparkleberry fails in SW Florida landscapes.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Requires acidic soil — confirm your site is appropriate before purchasing.
plants.expert_tips: Sparkleberry is rarely planted but genuinely beautiful especially in older specimens with their distinctive flaking reddish bark. The spring flowers are delicate and beautiful, the fall berries attract birds, and the bark provides year-round interest. Worth the extra effort of soil preparation.
plants.fun_fact: Sparkleberry is in the same genus as blueberries, huckleberries, and cranberries. The berries are edible but extremely astringent — they are essentially left to wildlife, which suits them perfectly.
plants.traditional_uses: Berries used in folk medicine as an astringent. Wood used for small tool handles by some Native American peoples.
plants.conservation_notes: One of the few native acid-soil plants of SW Florida's scrub and flatwood habitats. These ecosystems are among the most threatened in the state.

plants.description: Native coastal hammock tree with clusters of small grape-like fruits beloved by white-crowned pigeons and mockingbirds. Edible for humans — small and tart. Very salt and drought tolerant.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth. Slower than sea grape.
plants.pruning_notes: Can be maintained as a specimen tree or large shrub.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy in coastal SW Florida. Extremely salt and drought tolerant.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, bird food critical for white-crowned pigeons, mammals, coastal habitat
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe purple berries. Clean and sow fresh.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed much better than dried.
plants.transplant_notes: Very easy to transplant. Tolerates coastal exposure well.
plants.looks_like_notes: Pigeon plum has smaller, narrower leaves than sea grape. The bark is rougher and more textured. Smaller growth habit. Fruit clusters are similar but smaller.
plants.attracts_specific: White-crowned pigeon (primary consumer — critical food source), Mockingbird, Raccoon
plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Less common than sea grape.
plants.expert_tips: Pigeon plum is specifically named for the white-crowned pigeon — a beautiful bird that has experienced significant population declines as its coastal hammock food sources have been reduced by development. Planting pigeon plum is a direct conservation action for this species.
plants.fun_fact: White-crowned pigeons, which depend heavily on pigeon plum fruit, fly up to 100 miles daily between their nesting grounds in the Florida Keys and feeding areas on the mainland. Each pigeon plum planted in SW Florida is a potential refueling stop on this remarkable daily journey.
plants.traditional_uses: Fruit edible for humans — tart and small but palatable. Used in jams in some Caribbean cultures.
plants.conservation_notes: White-crowned pigeon populations have declined significantly with the loss of coastal hammock habitat. Pigeon plum is one of their most important food sources.

plants.description: Attractive native hammock tree with glossy pinnate leaves and clusters of small purple-black fruits that many birds eat. Fast-growing and good for quick canopy. Interesting compound leaves give a tropical appearance.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing native hammock tree
plants.pruning_notes: Minimal pruning. Remove dead wood only.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Fast growing and low maintenance in well-drained sites.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, bird and mammal food from fruits, fast canopy establishment
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe purple-black fruits. Clean and sow fresh.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates readily.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well from container. Fast growing once established.
plants.looks_like_notes: The compound pinnate leaves and clusters of small purple-black fruits on reddish stalks are identifying. Attractive tropical appearance year-round.
plants.attracts_specific: Migratory warblers (fruit), Northern mockingbird, Various frugivorous birds
plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at select native plant nurseries. Worth seeking out for fast canopy establishment.
plants.expert_tips: Paradise tree is one of the best native trees for quickly establishing a canopy in a restoration planting or new landscape. Its fast growth combined with genuine wildlife value makes it an excellent choice when immediate results are needed.
plants.fun_fact: The seeds of Simarouba glauca contain 55-70% oil and have been researched extensively as a biodiesel crop in tropical regions. The oil quality rivals olive oil for cooking.
plants.traditional_uses: Seeds are pressed for edible oil in Central America and India. The oil is also used medicinally and for soap making.
plants.conservation_notes: A tree of tropical hammocks increasingly rare in SW Florida due to habitat loss.

plants.description: Often overlooked but highly valuable native coastal hammock tree. Small red fruits are an important food source for migrating warblers and vireos. One of the few native trees that tolerates shade well. Very salt tolerant.
plants.growth_notes: Slow growing coastal hammock tree
plants.pruning_notes: Minimal pruning needed. Tolerates shaping.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Excellent once established but slow growing and specific to well-drained sites.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, migratory bird fruit, nesting, shade tolerant — rare trait in coastal natives
plants.propagation_seed: Collect red fruits when soft. Clean and sow fresh in well-drained mix.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed performs much better than stored.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants reasonably well from container. Plant in well-drained site. Tolerates partial shade — unusual for coastal species.
plants.looks_like_notes: Blolly identified by its small oval leaves, reddish new growth, and bright red berry clusters attractive to birds. The shade tolerance distinguishes it from most coastal natives.
plants.attracts_specific: Migratory warblers (red berries critical during fall migration), Red-bellied woodpecker, Gray catbird

seasonal_care.august: Berries ripening — peak migrant bird activity

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at select native plant nurseries. Often overlooked but highly recommended by Lee County Extension.
plants.expert_tips: Blolly is specifically recommended by the Lee County Extension as an underused native for coastal SW Florida landscapes. Its shade tolerance makes it invaluable for planting in the understory of larger coastal trees.
plants.fun_fact: Blolly is listed as a 'bird magnet' by the Florida Ornithological Society during fall migration. The red berries ripen precisely when migratory warblers and other migrants are moving through SW Florida.
plants.traditional_uses: Limited documented traditional uses.
plants.conservation_notes: A declining component of SW Florida's coastal hammock habitat. Each planted specimen contributes to preserving this tree in the landscape.

plants.description: Enormously productive in SW Florida. Leaves, pods, seeds, and flowers all edible and highly nutritious. Grows extremely fast. Straight trunks useful as garden stakes. Prune hard regularly to keep productive and manageable.
warnings: Leaves typically eaten cooked or dried rather than raw in large quantities.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: Rapid growth and informal appearance may conflict with HOA aesthetic standards.

plants.description: Breathtaking tree with clouds of lavender-purple tubular flowers in spring. Feathery fern-like foliage attractive even when not in bloom. Less salt tolerant so better for inland properties. Not invasive in FL.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing ornamental tree
plants.pruning_notes: Prune only dead or crossing branches. The feathery canopy is the ornamental feature.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy in inland SW Florida in well-drained soil. Salt sensitive — inland sites only.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bee and butterfly forage from flowers, attractive seasonal ornamental
plants.propagation_seed: Collect flat winged seeds from pods. Sow fresh in well-drained mix.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh seed in well-drained sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Germination generally good with fresh seed.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well when young. Plant inland — not salt tolerant. Full sun required.
do_not_plant_near: Coastal and beachfront properties — not salt tolerant
plants.looks_like_plants: Blue jacaranda (same species — only one commonly planted)
plants.looks_like_notes: Jacaranda is unmistakable when in bloom — clouds of lavender-purple flowers before the leaves emerge. The feathery bipinnate leaves are also distinctive.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybees (flowers), Native bees, Butterflies

seasonal_care.june: Rainy season growth — full leaf canopy

common_problems.symptoms: Good leaf growth but few or no flowers
common_problems.solution: Jacaranda flowers best with a pronounced dry period. SW Florida's dry season usually provides this. Overwatering or irrigating through the dry season can reduce flowering. Reduce or eliminate irrigation November-February.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and garden centers.
plants.expert_tips: Jacaranda flowers before its leaves emerge in spring — the entire tree appears covered in purple before a single leaf is visible. Plant it where you can see the full canopy effect, ideally with morning light behind it.
plants.fun_fact: Jacaranda is considered one of the world's most beautiful flowering trees and appears in countless famous cityscapes including Pretoria South Africa, Buenos Aires Argentina, and Lisbon Portugal.
plants.traditional_uses: The bark of jacaranda has been used medicinally in South American traditional medicine. No significant food uses.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no significant invasive concerns in SW Florida.

plants.description: One of the most commonly planted shade trees in SW Florida. Dense evergreen canopy provides excellent shade and bird nesting habitat. Very hurricane resistant. Salt and drought tolerant. Slow growing but extremely long-lived.
plants.growth_notes: Slow growing but extremely long-lived
plants.pruning_notes: Prune only dead wood. Strong natural form requires no shaping.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very low maintenance. Slow growth is its primary limitation.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bird nesting and food, dense shade canopy
plants.propagation_seed: Not commonly propagated from seed. Usually purchased as container grown stock.
plants.germination_notes: Not typically grown from seed in home landscape context.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well from container. Very drought and salt tolerant once established. Slow to establish.
do_not_plant_near: Areas where its eventual large size would be a problem — slow growing but gets very large
plants.looks_like_notes: Black olive is not an olive tree at all — no olives. The common name comes from the small olive-like fruits. The dense evergreen canopy and strong branch structure are distinctive.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Very widely available at SW Florida nurseries and garden centers.
plants.expert_tips: Black olive is one of the most reliable large shade trees for SW Florida — extremely hurricane resistant, salt tolerant, and long-lived. The slow growth is frustrating but the eventual result is one of the most dependable large canopy trees available.
plants.fun_fact: Despite the common name, black olive (Bucida buceras) is completely unrelated to the true olive (Olea europaea) and produces no edible fruit. The name came from the vaguely olive-like appearance of its small fruits.
plants.traditional_uses: The dense hard wood is used for construction and furniture in its native range in the Caribbean and Central America.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native but widely used and not considered invasive in SW Florida.

plants.description: Stunning ornamental with large velvety deep purple flowers and soft fuzzy leaves. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit frequently. Not salt tolerant — better for inland properties.

plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bee butterfly and hummingbird forage, stunning ornamental

plants.germination_notes: Cuttings are the standard propagation method.

do_not_plant_near: Coastal salt-spray areas — not salt tolerant. Alkaline soil without amendment.
plants.looks_like_notes: The large velvety deep purple flowers with prominent stamens and soft fuzzy leaves are distinctive and unmistakable.

common_problems.symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis, poor growth
common_problems.solution: Usually iron deficiency from alkaline soil. Apply chelated iron and sulfur to lower soil pH. Use acidifying fertilizer. This is the primary challenge of growing tibouchina in SW Florida.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and garden centers.
plants.expert_tips: Tibouchina needs slightly acidic soil to perform at its best in SW Florida — if yours is turning yellow, the soil pH is too high. Apply sulfur and chelated iron as a rescue treatment, then switch to an acidifying fertilizer for ongoing maintenance.
plants.fun_fact: Tibouchina flowers contain a natural purple dye that has been used in traditional textile dyeing in South America.
plants.traditional_uses: Used medicinally in Brazilian folk medicine for various conditions. Bark extracts studied for antimicrobial properties.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no significant invasive concerns in SW Florida.

plants.description: Spectacular tree cascading with long hanging clusters of bright yellow flowers in spring. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers actively. Birds eat the seeds.
warnings: Toxic to pets and livestock — all parts especially seed pods are toxic. The pulp is used medicinally but should never be self-administered.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing spectacular flowering tree
plants.pruning_notes: Prune only dead wood. The weeping branch habit is the ornamental feature.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy in SW Florida's heat with good drainage. Drought tolerant once established.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bee and butterfly forage, bird seed, beautiful seasonal ornamental

plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well when young. Full sun required. Excellent drainage essential.
do_not_plant_near: Pet and livestock areas — all parts including pods are toxic
plants.looks_like_notes: Golden shower tree identified by its spectacular pendulous clusters of pure yellow flowers and very long (1-2 ft) cylindrical dark brown seed pods. Unmistakable when in bloom.

common_problems.problem: Toxic seed pods accessible to pets
common_problems.symptoms: Pet illness after ingesting pods or seeds

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries.
plants.expert_tips: Golden shower tree puts on one of the most spectacular flower displays available in SW Florida — cascading yellow clusters so dense the flowers can obscure the foliage entirely. For maximum impact, site it where you can see it from inside your home during its spring bloom.
plants.fun_fact: Golden shower tree is the national tree of Thailand and is used in Thai New Year celebrations. The flowers appear on Thai national documents and symbols.
plants.traditional_uses: The pulp inside the seed pods is used medicinally as a laxative throughout tropical Asia. Used in Ayurvedic medicine for thousands of years. The wood is used for furniture and small carved items.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native but widely planted ornamental. The African tulip tree (a serious invasive) is sometimes confused with flowering trees like golden shower — always verify species before planting.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries.
plants.expert_tips: Hong Kong orchid tree blooms when almost nothing else does — its fall and winter flowering season fills the gap left by summer-blooming plants. Combined with its butterfly-shaped leaves and orchid-like flowers it is one of the most distinctive landscape trees available.
plants.fun_fact: Hong Kong orchid tree was discovered in 1880 as a single tree growing near an abandoned house site in Hong Kong. It is a sterile hybrid of two other Bauhinia species that occurred naturally. Every Hong Kong orchid tree on earth is a clone descended from that single wild discovery.
plants.traditional_uses: No significant traditional uses.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental. The sterile nature means no invasive seed dispersal — making it more ecologically responsible than seeding Bauhinia species.

plants.description: Iconic symmetrical conifer widely planted in SW Florida as a living Christmas tree and landscape specimen. Very salt tolerant. Birds nest in the branches and eat seeds from cones. Grows tall and narrow — good for tight spaces.

plants.propagation_cutting: Not practical — grows true from seed but slow.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh seed in well-drained mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates better than stored.

do_not_plant_near: Do not remove central leader — permanently ruins the tree's form
plants.looks_like_notes: Norfolk Island pine identified by its distinctive perfectly symmetrical layered branch pattern. Horizontal branches in distinct whorls, soft short dark green needles. Unmistakable in landscape.

plants.expert_tips: Norfolk Island pine is sold by the millions as living Christmas trees in the US. After Christmas, many end up in the landscape — they can eventually grow 50-100 ft tall. Consider the eventual size before planting one from your holiday display.
plants.fun_fact: Norfolk Island pines are not true pines — they belong to an ancient family that has remained essentially unchanged for over 200 million years. They were used by early Pacific navigators to identify Norfolk Island from far at sea.
plants.traditional_uses: The seeds of Norfolk Island pine were eaten by indigenous peoples of Norfolk Island. The wood is used for furniture and construction in the Pacific.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental widely planted in SW Florida. No significant invasive concerns.

plants.description: Tropical tree with intensely fragrant yellow-green star-shaped flowers used in perfumery — the scent is extraordinary. Blooms nearly year-round. Bees and hummingbirds visit. Grows very fast into a large weeping-form tree.

plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bee and hummingbird forage, extraordinary fragrance

plants.traditional_uses: Flowers used in hair oil and as fragrant decorations for beds in Southeast Asian wedding traditions. The essential oil is used therapeutically in aromatherapy.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no significant invasive concerns in SW Florida.
